Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The lamp on the desk burns with a dry, peppery smell, turning the brass edge of the Garvey signet warm against the dark wood. Beside it, a blue-paper primer lies among the clothes the lawyers sent ahead. Its gilt title catches the light whenever the flame bends: *A First Guide to the Conclave of Thrones.*

Across from the bed, the framed letter has been hung a little too high, as if whoever arranged the room thought it belonged to the house more than to its intended reader. The ink is brown with age. *To my great-nephew, should one ever come to Garvey House—* The rest disappears beneath the frame's narrow lower rail.

A bell sounds somewhere below: not grand enough for chapel, but clear enough to travel through the old timber and plaster. A moment later, the house begins answering it. Chairs scrape in the floor beneath this one. Someone laughs in the corridor, then a door shuts with deliberate care.

At the threshold, a young man pauses without crossing it. He is tall, impeccably dressed in a dark green coat cut close through the shoulders, with fine dark fur visible over the backs of his hands where they rest on a folded sheet of paper. His amber eyes flick once toward the letter, then return to you with the practiced courtesy of someone who has had to make courtesy look effortless.

"Rowan Garvey?" he asks. "I am Rashid vel Amara. Dinner is downstairs, and the dining hall has enough doors to make a first arrival feel like a tactical error. I was headed that way."

Behind him, the corridor opens onto a stairwell washed in candlelight. Voices drift upward with the smell of roast citrus and something peppery enough to compete with the lamp oil. The folded paper in Rashid's hand is covered in closely set names, most of them crossed out in a precise black line.

He tucks it into an inner pocket. "Would you like company on the way down?"

exchanges.player: "Yes, thank you." I go downstairs with Rashid. On the way I ask him, "Do you know whether any of the professors knew the Garveys?"
exchanges.story:
The stairwell narrows around its turn, old dark wood giving way to pale stone at the ground floor. Rashid takes the inside of the curve without seeming to choose it. The list from his pocket makes a soft, repeated tap against his coat as he walks.

“Professor Stone is the likeliest person to ask,” he says. “He teaches human Covenant history, and he is usually in the library after dinner; whether he knew your family himself, I cannot tell you. Ashworth has been chancellor for sixty years, but I have never found him generous with old stories.”

At the foot of the stairs, he glances toward the library's half-open door, where a lamp burns beyond the ironwork. “Stone may have an answer worth having. Or he may have a reason not to.”

The dining hall is already bright with candlelight and the steadier glow of working lamps. Seven places along the long table have been set with the same white plates and different drinking vessels: a broad black stone cup at one end, a narrow silver goblet at another, a clear green glass that catches the flame in its stem.

Several heads turn as Rashid enters with you. A tall woman with swept-back black-red horns has claimed a seat halfway down the table, her severe black hair catching a red shine from the candles. Beside the window, a white-haired woman sits so still that the frost-pale outline of her profile seems carved into the chair. A silver-haired elf has a small book open beside her plate, one finger marking a page; she closes it without hurry.

Near the far end, an angel in white and gold is saying something low to a smaller woman with blue-black hair and entirely black eyes. The angel's voice reaches the doorway in the tail end of a line: “—and the wording is still an excuse.” Across from them, another angel straightens a folded napkin with exacting care.

Rashid pauses beside an empty chair, then looks toward the table. “Everyone, this is Rowan Garvey.”

exchanges.player: "Good evening. I'm Rowan." I greet the others, take the empty chair, and help myself to dinner. I listen to the conversation.
exchanges.story:
Your greeting passes around the table with the small pause reserved for a name everyone has heard before meeting its owner. The horned woman inclines her head once. “Ashara vel Kothren.” The white-haired woman offers Ysolde Thornmantle; the elf, after a glance from you to the signet, gives Caelindra Vaeyn in a voice as smooth as the varnished table. Thessaly Morrow lifts her green glass in acknowledgement, while Aldric Verantus rises far enough from his chair to make the courtesy formal.

Seraphel's smile reaches her blue eyes as she opens one hand toward the empty place. “Good evening, Rowan Garvey—\nSit and be fed.”

A server in Academy livery sets down covered dishes: rice steamed with saffron and nuts, slices of dark-crusted fish in a citrus glaze, charred greens shining with oil. The heat rising from Ashara's place makes the nearest candle lean away from her plate. Rashid waits until you have served yourself before drawing out the folded sheet from his coat and laying it beside his glass.

“I am collecting names for supervised evening access to the covered court while the faculty decides what actually happened,” he says. “The present ban has shut out students who cannot pay for private training.”

Aldric's fingers remain on his folded napkin. “I will not sign a request concerning an injury until I have seen the instructor's report.”

Ashara takes a piece of fish with the point of her knife. “Then read the report,” she says. “Do not mistake an unanswered question for a reason to punish everyone who uses the court.”

Rashid's mouth tightens for a moment before he writes something beside one of the names on his sheet. He does not press her about the individual booking she has for tomorrow. Across the table, Thessaly reaches for the paper when it comes near her, reading the first lines with her head tilted. Caelindra takes another measured bite of dinner and watches the exchange over the rim of her glass. Ysolde's attention has settled on the covered dish nearest her, where the steam has begun to cloud the silver lid.

The disagreement does not fill the room so much as give it a current. Cutlery resumes its quiet work around it; outside the tall windows, the garden lamps have begun to kindle along the pale paths.

exchanges.player: I finish dinner and leave the court dispute to the people who know more about it. In my room, I take down the framed letter, carefully open the back, and read the whole thing. I replace it in the frame afterward, then go to the library to look for Professor Stone.
exchanges.story:
Dinner runs on after the first disagreement has lost its sharpest edge. Rashid keeps his petition beside his plate, speaking with Thessaly in low tones when she returns it; Aldric eventually excuses himself toward the chapel. Ashara remains at the table long enough to finish her wine, while Caelindra's book reappears at her elbow between courses. By the time the last plates are cleared, the garden beyond the windows has gone dark except for the lamps along its paths.

Upstairs, the frame comes down from the wall with a faint dry rasp of brass hook against plaster. Its backing is held by small bent tabs. When they are eased aside, the painted board lifts free to reveal a sheet of cream paper tucked flat behind it, folded twice and softened at the creases.

The handwriting is the same brown, sloping hand visible through the frame.

*My dear great-nephew,*

*If you have found this, then our long line of improbabilities has produced you at last. I had it framed because a letter in a drawer is treated as property; a letter on a wall becomes decoration, which is how important things are often kept safe.*

*The house is yours in the precise sense that its roof and debts are yours. The people who eat beneath it are not. Give them room, food if it is wanted, and the right to decline you. The Council has suffered enough from people mistaking obligation for affection.*

*You will hear the Garveys praised for being useful. Be useful only when you mean to be; usefulness becomes a leash when someone else fastens it for you.*

*Keep notes in your own hand: dates, names, exact words. Ask who has seen the original. But do not let every kindness become a clue. It is possible for a person to want nothing from you except your company, and I hope you find such people.*

*If a day at the Academy feels too large, come home to dinner. The house should be good for that much.*

*Your affectionate great-aunt,*

*Miriam Garvey*

The paper settles back into its hiding place without resistance. Once the frame is restored, Miriam's first visible line returns to its old place above the bed, giving nothing away.

The library is quieter than the dining hall, with lamp-oil air and the occasional soft tick of cooling metal from the spiral stair. Most of its tables are empty. At one near the ground-floor windows, a human man with iron-grey hair sits beneath a green-shaded lamp, reading a wide volume whose margins are crowded with smaller, neater handwriting. A plain cup of tea has gone cold at his elbow.

He looks up as you approach. His eyes find the signet, then your face. After a moment, he closes the book over one marked page.

“Mr. Garvey,” Professor Gareth Stone says. “What are you looking for?”

exchanges.player: "I've just read a letter my great-aunt Miriam left for me. Did you know her? I'd like to hear what she was like from someone who met her."
exchanges.story:
The name holds Professor Stone still for a beat. He takes off his spectacles and folds them with both hands before setting them atop the closed book.

“Miriam Garvey,” he says. “Yes. I knew her well enough to be corrected by her, which was how she preferred to be remembered.”

He leans back in his chair, looking for a moment not at the shelves but at the rain-dark window beyond them. “She worked first in the human delegation's correspondence office, and later taught source reading here when I was still young enough to think a full archive was the same thing as understanding it. Miriam had a remarkable gift for making the rest of us feel lazy.”

One memory seems to settle into place. “There was a seminar on the First Transit Accord. A dragon student announced that the human text was merely a translation, and that the elven original was therefore the only version worth consulting. Miriam did not argue. She gave every student a copy in each available script and asked them to find the clause about safe passage.”

Stone's mouth shifts, almost a smile. “They spent an hour at it. The elven wording concerned tolls. The angel wording concerned conduct. The human version had been drafted to carry both meanings, because the negotiators had known exactly where later governments would try to make a gap. Miriam's point was not that one language was truer than another. It was that calling something a translation could be a convenient way to stop reading.”

He reaches for the cold tea, then sets it down again without drinking. “The dragon student came back the next morning with a better question. Miriam gave him plum cake from her desk drawer and told him that improvement ought to be rewarded before it became a habit.”

His gaze returns to you. “She was exacting, funny when she forgot to be careful, and impatient with anyone who treated people as furniture in an argument. She was not always easy. She would have disliked being made into a saint.”

Stone moves a stack of books from the other side of the table, clearing a space beneath the lamp.

exchanges.player: I sit down. "I wish I'd met her. Did she ever talk about my parents? They died when I was small, and I never heard any of this growing up."
exchanges.story:
Stone's expression changes at the mention of your parents, the almost-smile leaving it without quite becoming solemnity. He draws his cold cup closer, more for something to do with his hands than for the tea.

“She did, though she wrote about them more freely than she spoke,” he says. “I met them once, here, when you were still small enough to sleep through a library. Miriam said they wanted you to have an ordinary childhood before the Conclave was allowed to claim any part of you.”

It had been a wet afternoon, Stone explains, and the two of them arrived with a small leather box of water-damaged household papers. One spent most of the visit asking whether the maps inside could be dried without losing the pencil marks; the other found a children's history left on a nearby chair and began correcting its captions in the margin with an ordinary graphite pencil. Miriam had been exasperated by both of them and plainly pleased to have them near.

From her letters, he knew more of their daily life than of their plans. She wrote that one of them repaired things long after anyone sensible would have replaced them: hinges, clocks, a kettle that whistled at the wrong pitch. The other kept names in a pocket notebook—neighbors, teachers, the children who came to the door for lessons—because forgetting a name was, in Miriam's view, a small failure of manners. When she described the two together, she tended to make them sound busy, untidy, and capable of turning a modest supper into an occasion.

Stone rests a finger on the book's worn cover. “That is not the whole of them. It is only what I saw, and what Miriam chose to tell me.”

Beyond the green-shaded lamp, the library shelves rise into shadow. The book he had been reading remains closed between you, its marker ribbon caught at the edge of the pages.

exchanges.player: I take a moment before answering. "That's more than I had when I sat down. Thank you. Do you still have her letters? If they aren't too private, I'd be grateful to read the parts about my parents sometime, and perhaps copy a little for myself."
exchanges.story:
Stone considers the request without looking away. At last, he nods once.

“I do still have them,” he says. “You may read the passages about your parents and copy what you wish in your own hand; the rest belongs to a woman who trusted me, and I will not make all of it public merely because she is gone.”

He opens a shallow drawer beneath the table and takes out a blank library slip. In a careful, compact script, he writes *Miriam Garvey — personal correspondence*, then adds a time beneath it.

“I keep the packet in my rooms rather than on these shelves. I will bring it here tomorrow evening, after the dinner bell.”

The slip remains on the table between the closed history and the cold cup. It is not an official summons or a stamped permission—only a name, a place, and a promise made in ink.

exchanges.player: I take the slip. "Tomorrow evening, then. Thank you for trusting me with that much. Good night, Professor." I leave him to his reading and return to the dining hall to see whether anyone is still about. I'd enjoy a cup of tea and a little company before bed.
exchanges.story:
Professor Stone acknowledges your good night with a small inclination of his head, then reopens the history beneath the green lamp. By the time you leave the library, he is reading again, one hand keeping the marker ribbon in place.

The dining hall has thinned to its after-hours shape. The servers have cleared the plates and most of the candles, leaving only a pair of lamps burning over the middle of the long table. At the window end, Ysolde Thornmantle remains in her place from dinner. A small iron teapot sits on a trivet before her with two plain cups beside it, and she has turned one of the chairs to face the gardens rather than the table.

Beyond the glass, the lamps along the pale paths shine steadily while the light bridges flare and fade over the storm below. Ysolde watches them with her hands folded around her cup. When she notices you in the doorway, she glances at the unused place setting, then reaches for the teapot.

“There is enough,” she says. “It is mountain mint. Would you like some?”

exchanges.player: "Yes, please." I sit beside Ysolde and accept a cup, watching the light bridges for a while. "Do you ever get used to that view?"
exchanges.story:
Ysolde fills the second cup with a careful, level pour. The tea is pale gold and sharp with mint, its steam briefly whitening the window before it vanishes.

For a while, the hall contains only the small sound of the pot settling on its trivet and the distant pulse of light beyond the gardens. The westward bridge brightens, thins to a line, then broadens again over the storm.

“No,” Ysolde says at last. “I have seen it from above, from the spans, and from this window in every season. It changes each time.”

She raises one finger toward the west bridge as its light takes on a faint green cast near the far end. “That color arrives before the wind reaches the gardens. The storm will climb for an hour, then fall away.”

Her gaze stays on the bridge. “Getting used to it would mean ceasing to look.”

exchanges.player: I settle back with my tea and stay by the window for another half hour, watching for the wind to reach the gardens. I'm comfortable sitting quietly.
exchanges.story:
The tea cools slowly between your hands. Outside, the bridge lights keep their measured brightening and dimming while the garden lamps hold steady along the paths.

Ysolde does not seem to require speech to fill the interval. Once, she rises to adjust the lid of the teapot; once, she traces a short line through the condensation on the window and watches it vanish. The dining hall remains otherwise empty, its far end receding into polished shadow.

Near the end of the half hour, the green at the far end of the west bridge deepens. A moment later, the leaves in the nearest garden bed turn their pale undersides toward the glass. The wind arrives without thunder, pressing a cool hand along the walls of Garvey House and stirring the candle flame beside the unused places at the table.

Ysolde watches it pass through the gardens. “There,” she says.

exchanges.player: "I'll watch for that green next time. Thank you for the tea, Ysolde. Good night." I return to my room, write down what Stone told me while it is fresh, and put his slip somewhere I'll see it tomorrow. Then I go to bed. In the morning, I get dressed and come down for breakfast.
exchanges.story:
Ysolde inclines her head over the last of her tea. “Good night, Rowan.”

In your room, the lamp gives the desk a small circle of certainty against the dark windows. Stone's account of Miriam, the water-damaged papers, the corrected captions, and the ordinary details of your parents' life take their places on the page before the edges can blur. The library slip goes beside the blue primer, where its compact writing will meet the eye on the way out.

The house settles around you after the lamps are put out: a distant stair creaks, pipes knock once in the wall, and then the storm's slow pressure is all that remains beyond the glass.

Morning finds the gardens washed pale beneath a high grey light. By the time you reach the ground floor, Garvey House smells of toasted oats, coffee, and the orange peel someone has dropped into a warming pot of tea.

Breakfast has begun in the dining hall without the ceremony of the previous evening. Thessaly sits near the sideboard with a small grid of painted wooden tiles arranged before her, turning one over in her fingers as she studies the possible moves. At the long table, Rashid has claimed a place with a bowl of porridge and a notebook opened beside it. He looks up when you enter, then closes the notebook without covering the page.

“Morning,” he says. “The porridge is better than it looks.”

exchanges.player: "Morning. I found Professor Stone last night, by the way. Thank you for pointing me to him." I help myself to porridge and coffee, then look at the tiles. "Thessaly, what are you playing? Could you teach me when you've finished this round?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid's expression eases as he reaches for his coffee. “I am glad you found him. Stone is better company once he decides a question deserves an answer.”

The porridge is thick with toasted oats and a little honey, and the coffee has been brewed strong enough to cut through the morning's damp chill. At the sideboard, Thessaly looks up from the tiles as you address her. One pale blue piece rests between two darker ones, its painted path ending at the edge of the grid.

“It is Seven Paths,” she says. “You turn one tile each move and must connect every border gate to the center without sending a road back across itself; yes, I will teach you when this round is finished.”

She studies the blue tile again, then sets one fingertip beside it without moving it. The empty chair across from her has been pulled a little clear of the sideboard.

exchanges.player: I take the chair and finish breakfast while watching her round. When she is ready to teach me, I listen and try a practice round myself, working inward from one border gate at a time. I ask for help if I get stuck rather than pretending I understand.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly gives the blue tile one last quarter-turn. Its painted road curves into a pale lane, then into the small gold circle at the center of the grid. She traces each of the other border gates in turn with a fingernail, following their paths inward until she reaches the same circle.

“Finished,” she says.

She gathers the tiles into a neat pile and replaces the larger grid with a smaller board marked by four gates instead of seven. The central circle is fixed; around it, she lays out nine painted squares in a loose pattern of roads, forks, and blank ground. While you finish breakfast, she explains that each move turns a single tile, that every gate must reach the center, and that no route may cross itself or end on an unused edge.

Rashid finishes his coffee, slips his notebook into his coat, and leaves the dining hall with the quiet purpose he had brought to breakfast. Thessaly does not look up as the door closes. She squares the first tile toward you.

The practice board begins simply. Working from the nearest border gate, you turn a tile until its road runs inward, then shape the next one to meet it. A second gate joins the center by way of a forked square. On the fourth move, the remaining green route can be turned toward the open lane or toward the last unused fork; either choice appears to preserve the road in front of it.

When you ask for help, Thessaly leans closer but leaves the tile where it is. “Trace from the center this time,” she says. “The road you are saving has somewhere to go. The other one does not.”

From that direction, the dead end is visible: the open lane would leave the green gate stranded behind a turn that cannot be corrected later. The unused fork gives it a route around the central circle instead. With that tile turned, the last two paths settle into place one after the other.

Thessaly follows each route with her fingertip, checking the board in silence. Then she nudges the final tile a fraction straighter.

“That is a win,” she says. “The board does not care whether you asked for help.”

exchanges.player: I smile. "That's a forgiving board. Would you mind setting me another? I'll try looking from both ends this time." As I study the tiles, I ask, "Who taught you to play?"
exchanges.story:
Thessaly gathers the practice tiles before they can be disturbed by a passing sleeve. “It permits correction,” she says. “That is different from forgiving.”

She turns the pieces facedown, mixes them with quick, practiced movements, and lays out a fresh pattern with five border gates. This one has a narrow loop near the center and two forks placed close enough together to make the routes look simpler than they are.

“My cousin Rill taught me,” Thessaly says as she turns the first tile faceup. “She set the opening board badly on purpose and called it a lesson in attention; after three games, I stopped letting her arrange the first board.”

The last tile clicks into its place at the far edge of the grid. Thessaly straightens it with the side of one finger, then turns the board so the five gates face you.

exchanges.player: "I'll be sure to count the gates before playing Rill." I give the new board half an hour, tracing routes from the center as well as from the gates before each turn. When a move leaves a dead end, I go back and try another arrangement. I'd like to see how far I can get on my own this time.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly's black eyes rest on the board for a moment. “Count the gates twice,” she says. “Rill was very good at moving one when no one was looking.”

Then she folds her hands beside the sideboard and leaves the tiles to you.

The first few turns go slowly. From the central circle, one pale road can reach both the red and white gates if the near fork is left facing inward. The blue gate has only one usable entrance. The green gate appears to have two until a turn near the outer edge sends its path straight into blank ground.

That dead end takes the board apart again. The tiles return to their earlier positions one by one, and the next arrangement begins from the central loop rather than the nearest gate. A road that seemed wasted on the first attempt becomes the only clean route around the loop; the second fork gives the green gate its way in without cutting across the blue path.

By the time the half hour has passed, four gates reach the center. The fifth, set at the far edge, still points toward the wrong side of a narrow curve. Turning it closes the last road without disturbing the others.

The finished board holds together beneath the morning light: five painted routes, each continuous from its border gate to the gold circle in the middle.

Thessaly leans forward only then. She traces each path once, beginning from the center as you had, and gives a small nod.

“You counted,” she says.

exchanges.player: "Thank you for teaching me. I'd enjoy another game some morning." I stand and stretch, then fetch my notebook and a pencil from my room. I go out into the gardens for a slow walk, looking at the house from the paths. If I find a dry place to sit, I spend a while trying to sketch it.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly begins sorting the tiles into their small cloth bag. “Some morning,” she says. “Do not expect me to make the first board gentle.”

The gardens hold the morning's dampness in their leaves, but the paths are dry beneath the pale sheltering walls. From there, Garvey House looks less like a single building than an old agreement that has acquired additions without ever quite settling the argument. Dark lower stone rises beneath white, inward-curving window frames; above them, a second-floor bay is wrapped in weathered timber that has grown around its own iron brackets. The upper windows catch the grey light in uneven ranks.

Past a bed of late-blooming blue flowers, a covered stone bench sits beneath the overhang of a narrow arcade. The wind reaches the garden only in softened breaths there, carrying the sharp green scent of clipped hedges rather than the storm's colder air.

With the notebook open across your knees, the first pencil lines find the roofline, then the taller chimney at the north end, then the curve of the bay window above your room. The proportions resist a simple outline. One side of the house leans into the garden; the other seems to turn away toward the library and the unused upper floors. A path and its low wall take shape beneath it, followed by the dark mass of the lower stone.

For a while, the only interruptions are the scrape of pencil on paper and the small movements of leaves along the arcade. The house remains in view beyond the page, larger and stranger than the sketch, but held there in a beginning of lines.

exchanges.player: I finish my sketch, then spend the rest of the day getting settled and reading the blue primer. I check the time on Stone's slip so I can plan dinner around it. When my appointment is due, I take my notebook and pencil to the library to meet him.
exchanges.story:
The sketch ends with the arcade's shadow falling across the lower wall, a darker wash of pencil beneath the unsteady lines of the upper windows. Back inside, clothes find drawers, books find a place on the desk, and the room gradually loses the look of an arrangement made for a stranger.

The blue primer gives the Covenant in a clean sequence of dates and principles: the end of the Sundering War, the Council's seven seats, the bridges and treaties that followed, the Academy's charge to teach future leaders before they inherit a crisis. Its account of the empty human seat is brief. Its pages on Conclave conduct are more exact, including Article Nineteen in the dry procedural language of law.

By late afternoon, the library slip still waits beside the primer, its appointment written beneath Miriam's name. The dinner bell is timed early enough to leave the ground-floor hall quiet again by the hour Stone set. When the lamps are lit in the library, you find him at the same window table beneath the green shade.

A grey linen packet rests beside his cold tea. It is tied with a faded blue ribbon, and several narrow paper markers stand from its edge.

“On time,” Stone says. “I found six of Miriam's letters that mention your parents; I marked the relevant passages, but left the pages whole. Context belongs to a letter, too.”

He unties the ribbon and sets the packet between you on the cleared table.

exchanges.player: "Thank you for bringing them." I sit down and carefully read the marked passages from all six letters, noting their dates. I copy the passages about my parents into my notebook in my own hand, taking my time with them.
exchanges.story:
The first marker leads to a letter dated **3 First Rain, 294**. Miriam writes that Tomas has “made a house of a place with a crooked roof,” and that Leona has learned every neighbor's name before deciding which of them is worth inviting to supper. In the margin, Miriam has added that Leona corrected the school register when it misspelled two children from the next street.

The next, dated **20 Sunheight, 295**, is shorter. Tomas and Leona are expecting a child. Miriam tells Stone that they have declined a formal visit to Garvey House: *They want one life that begins without a council chamber staring at it. I think that is sensible, though Tomas has never been sensible where a broken hinge is concerned.*

On **8 Frostfall, 296**, Miriam writes again: *Rowan is here. Tomas tried to repair the bassinet before he had learned how it was broken. Leona says the child will have an ordinary childhood, which is a promise worth keeping even if we have always been bad at ordinary.* The line is copied into the notebook beneath its date, the pencil pressure darkening slightly over the names.

The fourth marked passage, **14 Thaw, 298**, catches the library visit Stone remembers. Miriam describes the water-damaged maps, Tomas's insistence that the pencil annotations be preserved, and Leona finding errors in a children's history before the tea had cooled. *Rowan slept through the entire argument on Stone's shoulder,* she writes. *He was the most sensible person in the room.*

In the letter from **2 Harvest, 299**, Miriam complains fondly that Tomas has sent a kettle to be mended instead of buying a new one. She reports that Leona's pocket notebook now contains the names of twenty-three pupils, three grocers, and “at least one dog who has no business being included.” Then comes a quieter sentence: *They are determined you will know the world before you are asked to represent it.*

The final marker sits in a letter dated **19 First Rain, 300**. Miriam's handwriting is less even there. Tomas has been ill with a fever that breaks and returns; Leona is tired enough that she has stopped teaching for the week. The doctor calls it lingering and advises rest. *They mean to come when the weather improves,* Miriam writes. *For now, I have told them the house can wait.*

There is no later marked passage.

The six dates and their copied lines take up several pages of the notebook in your own hand. Across the table, Stone keeps the lamp steady over the correspondence and does not hurry the work.

exchanges.player: I sit with the last letter for a little while before closing my notebook. "Thank you. They feel a little nearer now." I leave the letters with Stone and wish him good night. Back in the hall, I look for Rashid. If I find him, I ask, "Have you had any word about your request for supervised court access?"
exchanges.story:
Stone receives the letters without gathering them too quickly. He reties the faded ribbon around the packet, sets it beside the green-shaded lamp, and returns your good night with a quiet courtesy before the book and correspondence reclaim the table.

The common room is warmer than the library, its oversized fireplace down to a bed of red coals. Rashid occupies one end of a study table beneath the dead Garvey portraits. A neat stack of papers lies before him: the request on top, signatures beneath, and an Academy notice weighted flat by an ink bottle.

He looks up when you ask about the court. “Enough for a meeting tomorrow at fourth bell; the court remains closed until the instructor's report is reviewed. Ashara signed, Aldric wants the report before his name joins, and the injured student's account will not be made public.”

Rashid slides the notice across the table just far enough to show the date and the dean's office seal. The request itself is written narrowly: supervised access, an explanation of the restriction, and a review after the report is available. No one name is made to carry the whole argument.

exchanges.player: I read the notice, then slide it back. "I'm glad you got a hearing. Is the meeting open to other students? I'd like to listen, if that's all right. I'm still learning how things get decided here."
exchanges.story:
Rashid reads the relevant line again before answering. “It is open. You need not ask my permission; any student may observe, though the signatories speak first and the clerk decides when the room has heard enough.”

He taps the final paragraph of the notice. The hearing will take place in a small office beside the covered court. The dean's representative will hear the request, receive the instructor's report when it is produced, and decide whether supervised access is possible before the broader restriction is reviewed.

“Come if you want to,” Rashid says. “It will not teach you everything about how decisions are made here, but it may teach you what people make them sound like.”

He draws the notice back into the stack and aligns its corners with the petition beneath it.

exchanges.player: "I'll come and listen. Good night, Rashid." I put my copied letters safely in my room and go to bed. The next day, after breakfast, I make my way to the office beside the covered court in time for fourth bell. I take a seat among the observers, keep notes, and stay through the meeting.
exchanges.story:
The office beside the covered court is narrow and bright, its frosted side window giving onto the empty packed earth beyond. A dozen chairs have been set in two uneven rows. Rashid sits at the small table nearest the dean's representative with his petition, while Ashara stands against the wall in a dark training coat, her reserved place at the court visible through the glass behind her. Aldric takes a seat among the observers. A clerk with an open ledger records the fourth bell as it sounds.

The hearing begins with the request read into the record: supervised evening access for students outside the Military track, an explanation of the present restriction, and review once the instructor's report is complete. Eighteen signatures follow it.

Rashid keeps his argument close to the page. “Students with private instruction have alternatives. The people who use the covered court do not all have that option, and a temporary safety measure should not become an indefinite exclusion because no one has finished asking what happened.”

The dean's representative asks whether anyone can establish the cause of the injury. Rashid says that he has an account from the student hurt, but was asked not to make that person a public example. The clerk writes this down without adding a name.

“The report before this office does not yet distinguish equipment failure, negligence, or ordinary training risk,” the representative says. “I will not reopen the court on inference.”

Ashara speaks only after the official invites additional comment. She does not offer her own booking as a substitute for the group, but she makes the narrower point that an individual reservation and a blanket suspension are separate decisions, each requiring a reason. Aldric says that he agrees the report should be produced promptly, though he will not support reopening the court until it is.

The discussion circles through supervision, cost, and who can reasonably be expected to attend an evening session. No answer comes that turns the injury into a simple fault. At the end, the representative orders a redacted preliminary summary of the instructor's report by noon the next day, invites confidential accounts to be added to the file, and sets a second hearing for two days hence. The court remains closed until then.

Your notes fill a page: eighteen signatures; no public witness; cause not established; report by noon; review at the second hearing. When the clerk closes the ledger, the observers begin to file out past the silent court.

exchanges.player: I return to Garvey House and spend the rest of the day reading and working on my sketch. At noon the next day, I go back to the court office and ask whether students can read the redacted preliminary summary. If it is available, I read it and note what it says.
exchanges.story:
The rest of the day at Garvey House passes quietly. The primer yields more names and procedures on a second reading; the sketch gains the darker join between the house's lower stone and its timbered upper story, then a few cautious leaves along the path. By evening, the court hearing has become a page of notes among other pages rather than the whole shape of the day.

At noon the following day, a fresh notice has been pinned outside the court office: **PRELIMINARY INCIDENT SUMMARY AVAILABLE FOR STUDENT INSPECTION.** The clerk behind the desk checks the timepiece on the wall, then brings out a single stamped copy when asked. It remains on the desk beneath a clear paperweight.

The summary identifies no student. It records that the injury occurred during an evening avoidance drill when the retaining pin on a suspended padded target gave way and the target swung unexpectedly into the participant's path. The injured student's wrist was treated at the infirmary.

An initial inspection found wear beneath the pin's enamel and an incomplete maintenance entry from the previous week. The report does not determine when the damage occurred, whether the instructor's pre-session check should have caught it, or whether the drill itself was being run within the proper staffing guidance. A full inspection of the covered court's equipment is ordered before any reopening.

The closing recommendation keeps the court shut for now, but distinguishes between repair of the target rig and the broader question of whether supervised access can resume once the equipment is cleared.

The notebook receives a new entry beneath the hearing notes: suspended target; worn retaining pin; maintenance record incomplete; no finding on supervision; full inspection pending; access question still open.

exchanges.player: I thank the clerk and check the notice for the second hearing's time before returning to Garvey House. I spend the afternoon and evening at home. The following day, I return to the office for that hearing, sit among the observers with my notebook, and stay through the meeting, taking notes as before.
exchanges.story:
The notice names the second hearing for fourth bell the following day. Its wording has changed since the first: **ACCESS REVIEW FOLLOWING PRELIMINARY INCIDENT SUMMARY.**

The afternoon and evening at Garvey House leave time for the primer, the sketch, and the ordinary creaks of the old residence. At fourth bell the next day, the office beside the covered court holds more people than before. The dean's representative and clerk have returned; a facilities officer has spread inspection sheets across the desk. Rashid sits with the petition. Ashara takes the wall again, and Aldric is among the observers with the preliminary summary folded in his hand.

The facilities officer reports that the failed target rig has been removed. The worn pin should have been caught in the previous maintenance check, though the inquiry has not yet determined who was responsible for that omission. The rest of the court's fixed equipment has passed an initial inspection, with two minor repairs scheduled before the following evening.

“The fault was in a piece of equipment,” Rashid says. “That is a reason to repair it and improve the check, not a reason to tell students without private instruction that they may simply do without practice.”

Ashara adds that a limited schedule can be tested without treating an individual booking as the Academy's whole answer. Aldric, after asking whether the supervising instructor will have authority to stop a session, says that he will support a trial if the safety conditions are written rather than assumed.

The dean's representative takes the point. Once the two repairs are certified, the court will reopen for a two-week pilot: three supervised evening sessions each week, twelve students per session, no participant fee, and a published sign-up list. The instructor will record equipment checks before and after each session. The confidential account from the injured student remains in the file but will not be circulated. The separate inquiry into the maintenance lapse continues.

The clerk reads the decision back into the ledger. In the notebook, the new page fills beneath the earlier hearing notes: rig removed; repairs due tomorrow; supervised pilot after clearance; twelve places; no fee; equipment checks logged; maintenance inquiry unresolved.

When the meeting ends, the office door opens onto the court's packed earth and its suspended targets, one space now empty where the failed rig had hung.

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The framed letter above the desk hangs crooked by the width of a fingernail. Beneath its glass, the opening address—*To my great-nephew, whom I never expected to know*—has browned more deeply than the rest of the page. Clothes sent ahead by people who know your measurements only from paperwork sit in careful stacks beside it. Ink darkens your fingers against the cuff of your carefully mended charcoal coat, and the Garvey signet catches the lamplight whenever your hand shifts.

The window looks over gardens already going blue at the edges. Pale paths wind between flowering walls; beyond them, a hard-light bridge holds a steady white line over the roiling cloudbank far below. The storm gives no thunder here. It only flashes now and then under the horizon, as if the world has remembered something it means to say later.

From downstairs comes the useful, ordinary noise of a house preparing to feed people: chair legs eased across old boards, a server calling for more bread, a burst of laughter cut off by a voice saying something too low to make out. Someone has opened the doors between the common room and the dining hall. Butter, pepper, and roast onions climb the stairwell with the warmth from the lamps.

A light knock sounds against the doorframe. A server in blue-and-silver Academy livery stands at the threshold, empty-handed for the moment.

“Mr. Garvey,” he says, “we are seating in a few minutes. The dining hall is down the main stair, through the common room. If you would like, I can show you the way.”

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I think I can follow the smell." I go downstairs and introduce myself. "Good evening. I'm Rowan." I take an empty seat and help myself to dinner.
exchanges.story:
The server steps aside, and the main stair carries you down through the house’s warmer layers: old wood, the edge of the common room’s fire, a lamp burning somewhere near the library door. Portraits in dark frames gather over the fireplace below, their painted Garveys looking past the stairs toward an age when the house held a family rather than a set of rooms.

The dining hall is brighter than the rest of it. Candles burn between working lamps along the long table, and the servers have filled the first bowls before everyone arrives. There are plenty of empty places among the seventeen settings. You take one and find the nearest dishes arranged for choice rather than ceremony: dark bread, roasted squash, a peppered lentil stew, and a platter of glazed onions that explains the smell upstairs.

At your greeting, the tall beastkin nearest the middle of the table rises just far enough to make the gesture clear. His cuffs sit perfectly over the fur at his wrists. “Rashid vel Amara—welcome to Garvey House.”

Beside him, the horned woman with ember-red skin has already claimed a bowl and set her napkin across her lap with military neatness. Her long black hair is tied severely back; her tail curves around the chair leg. “Ashara vel Kothren; eat while it is hot.”

Across the table, snow-pale Ysolde Thornmantle gives you a small inclination of her head, grey eyes briefly returning to the window. Caelindra Vaeyn’s violet gaze passes over the Garvey signet before she attends to her own place setting. Seraphel Dawnquill folds her small white wings more closely behind her chair, her warm gold light catching on the silver-haired elf’s goblet. Thessaly Morrow offers a quick, oddly timed smile from beneath blue-black hair, while Aldric Verantus straightens a fraction in his white-and-gold clothes and acknowledges you with a formal nod.

The stew is hot enough to steam the ink from no one’s fingers but yours, and the bread has a crisp blackened edge. Conversation starts again in a few low currents around the table. Rashid tears off a piece of his own loaf and looks across at you. “Did the primer tell you how we are meant to get through our first dinner?”

exchanges.player: "No. It explained quite a lot of ways to offend people, though." I eat some more stew, then ask Rashid, "What do you do for fun when you aren't being trained to run a country?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid tears a piece from his bread and considers it for just long enough that the question does not disappear into the table’s other talk. His amber eyes flick once toward Ashara.

“Practice, cards, and dinner with people who do not ask me to chair anything. I also enjoy an evening in which Ashara agrees with me once, though that is less common than a clean draw.”

Ashara’s tail taps the chair leg once. “Your definitions require revision.”

Rashid’s mouth turns at one corner as he reaches for the glazed onions. Across from him, Seraphel lowers her gaze to her bowl with the suggestion of a smile, while the storm flashes soundlessly beyond the gardens and turns the far wall of the dining hall briefly white.

exchanges.player: "Cards sounds good. If you're playing tonight, I'd like to join."
exchanges.story:
Rashid sets his bread down beside a folded sheet of notes that has acquired a faint crescent of stew at one corner.

“Then I will be playing. I have a petition to finish after dinner, but I can take a common-room table at nine. Bring whatever you are willing to lose.”

Thessaly’s black eyes move from Rashid to you and back again. Across the table, Ashara takes another spoonful of stew without looking up, while one of the servers refills the lamp nearest the window.

exchanges.player: I finish dinner, spend a little time reading my primer, and go to the common room at nine. I put five copper coins on the table. "That's as far as I'm going tonight. What are we playing?"
exchanges.story:
Dinner carries on around the long table until the lamps have burned lower and the first bowls have been traded for fruit and small cakes. Near the end, Rashid’s folded notes become a quiet argument instead of a piece of paper: he maintains that closing the covered court strands students who cannot pay for private instruction; Aldric holds that an injury deserves caution until someone has established what caused it; Ashara finds the restriction broad without offering up her own booked training time. Nothing settles before the plates are cleared. Rashid takes the notes away with him afterward.

Upstairs, the primer’s compact public history gives the Covenant the tidy shape of dates, articles, and civic virtues. Its pages on conduct devote far more care to possible insults than to ordinary conversation. By the time you set it aside, the house has quieted around the occasional stair creak and a door closing somewhere above.

At nine, the common room holds a low fire and the warm brass light of two lamps. Rashid is already at one of the study tables, his petition gone and a worn deck of cream-backed cards in its place. He has set out a shallow wooden dish for the coins. The five coppers land there with a modest, bright clatter.

He squares the deck against the tabletop. “Crossing: three cards each, one exchange before the reveal, and the hand nearest twenty-one wins unless it goes over. Five coppers is enough to teach the game without making an enemy of the evening.”

He shuffles with quick, exact hands, then deals three cards face down to each side of the table.

exchanges.player: "You'll have to tell me the card values. Let's play three hands, one copper apiece. For now, I'll exchange my largest card if my total is over twenty-one, and keep the hand otherwise."
exchanges.story:
Rashid places one of his own coppers beside the dish, then nudges one of yours to meet it.

“Fair enough: numbers count themselves, court cards count ten, and an ace may be one or eleven.”

The three cards on your side show a nine, an eight, and a seven. Twenty-four. The nine goes into the discard pile; the replacement is a four, leaving you at nineteen. Rashid studies his own hand without changing a card, then turns over a six, a five, and a nine.

Twenty.

He draws the two-copper pot to his side of the table and gathers the cards with neither apology nor ceremony. The second deal follows in the same quick rhythm, three fresh cards face down before you.

exchanges.player: I play the remaining two hands with the same rule: exchange my largest card if the total is over twenty-one, otherwise keep it. I stake one copper on each hand and stop after those two, as agreed.
exchanges.story:
For the second hand, the cards on your side make nineteen at once: a nine, an eight, and a two. Rashid’s make twenty-three. He gives up a court card for a four and finishes at seventeen, and the two-copper pot crosses the table to you.

The third hand asks more of the same rule. Your nine, eight, and seven make twenty-four; the nine goes into the discard pile, and a five brings the total down to twenty. Rashid keeps a court card, a six, and a five for twenty-one.

The last two coppers left unused in the wooden dish return to you. Rashid stacks the three finished hands into a neat square, two pots on his side of the table and one on yours. He is one copper ahead when the agreed game ends.

The fire has lowered to a red seam beneath its ash. Beyond the common-room windows, the gardens are dark except for their pale paths, and the hard-light bridge hangs motionless beyond them.

exchanges.player: I gather my remaining coins. "One copper for an evening's entertainment. I can live with that." I sit back. "How did you and Ashara meet? You seem well practised at winding each other up."
exchanges.story:
The remaining coins disappear into your hand. Rashid leaves his small winning stack where it is for the moment, one thumb resting on the squared deck.

“An Academy trial in Kothren territory, two years ago. I questioned one of her figures in a mock council, and she handed me a practice blade afterward to see whether I could challenge anything with my hands.”

He describes an afternoon in a false council chamber, where a group of prospective Conclave students had been given an invented dispute over a mountain pass and three hours to draft terms. Rashid had objected to the way Ashara’s proposal assigned control of the checkpoints; Ashara had answered the objection closely enough to leave no room for a second one before the proctor called time.

Afterward, in the covered practice court, she had passed him a wooden blade. The first exchange lasted long enough for him to discover that watching a ranked fighter and meeting one were separate skills. The second ended when the padded tip of her weapon touched the hollow below his jaw.

“Apparently, I could not,” Rashid says. “The problem is that she is usually worth arguing with.”

The cards sit between you in the quiet common room, their cream backs bright under the nearest lamp.

exchanges.player: I thank Rashid for the game and say good night. I sleep until morning, attend my classes the next day, and go to the public dueling ground after the last bell. If there is a bout underway, I watch from outside the rail until it finishes.
exchanges.story:
Rashid returns your good night with a nod and begins packing the deck before you are through the common-room doors.

Sleep passes without ceremony. In the morning, Conclave seminar begins beneath the framed Accords with Professor Windwhisper separating a dispute over Article Seven into the meanings of three nearly identical words. Practical Rhetoric follows in the afternoon, where Professor Kira has the room take opposing sides of a trade petition until the last bell releases everyone into the cooling light outside.

The public dueling ground is busy enough that a small crowd has gathered along the rail. Chalk on the ranking board gives the score before the action does: KOTHREN 2, VOSS 2. Inside the packed-earth octagon, Ashara faces a dark-haired dragon student with a long ash staff. The air around his weapon tugs dust into thin, circling lines. Heat shimmers close to Ashara’s blunted saber and the skin of her forearms.

Voss comes in with the staff high, then whips its butt toward her ribs on the turn. Ashara gives ground once, twice, her tail clearing the path of her heels. On the third step, she catches the staff just below its midpoint with her blade. A finger-width flare runs along the flat of the weapon, bright as a coal drawn from a fire.

Voss shifts his grip away from the heat. Ashara is already inside the staff’s reach. Her shoulder turns, her saber comes around, and its padded tip strikes the center of his chest before the gust around him can tighten again.

The referee’s raised hand brings the crowd’s noise up all at once. A runner changes the board to KOTHREN 3, VOSS 2. Ashara steps back and lowers her blade while Voss bows over the length of his staff, then the two of them leave the marked center to their respective sides of the rail.

exchanges.player: I wait until Ashara is no longer speaking to the referee, then approach without blocking her way. "Good bout. Would you like to have dinner with me tonight, just the two of us?"
exchanges.story:
The referee finishes recording the score and hands Ashara a strip of clean cloth for the sweat at her brow. She takes it, gives the board one brief look, and sets her blunted saber into its scabbard before turning from the rail.

At your invitation, she stops beside the equipment bench. Her gold eyes hold on you without wandering toward the dispersing crowd.

“Thank you. No; I do not know you well enough to spend an evening alone with you.”

She loops the cloth around the hilt guard, takes up her water flask, and heads toward the changing rooms along the outer edge of the ground.

exchanges.player: I stay beside the rail and call after her, "Just an hour? It might be a way to get to know each other."
exchanges.story:
Ashara stops at the edge of the equipment benches without turning back.

“An hour does not change my answer.”

Then she continues toward the changing rooms, the water flask knocking softly against the scabbard at her hip.

exchanges.player: I leave the grounds and spend the rest of the afternoon reading the primer in the library. At dinner I take a seat with the others and listen.
exchanges.story:
The library absorbs the rest of the afternoon in lamp-oil air and the hush of high shelves. The primer gives the Covenant its public sequence again—war, treaties, Council, Academy—then returns to the small hazards of address, seating, gifts, and promises. Light slips away from the reading tables before you reach the final page.

At dinner, Rashid has a clean copy of his request folded beside his plate. Ashara takes a seat farther down the table from him, her hair still damp at the ends from the changing rooms. The servers set out bowls of barley and greens while the other conversations find their places.

Rashid opens the paper. “I am submitting a request for supervised access in the morning: no names attached, and no verdict on the accident.”

Aldric sets down his spoon. “Give it to me after dinner. I will read it before I decide.”

“That is what reading is for,” Ashara says.

She draws the request toward herself, reads it through, and signs at the bottom with a decisive stroke. Rashid folds the paper once more after she passes it back. Around them, the meal resumes its quieter business of bread, lamps, and low talk.

exchanges.player: I leave the request to them. For the next two days I go to classes, work through the assigned reading, and spend my free afternoons sketching in the gardens. On the second evening I come down for dinner as usual.
exchanges.story:
The next two days acquire the Academy’s working rhythm. Morning bells pull students through the quadrangle in coats and uniforms; assigned reading fills the intervals between seminars with treaty clauses, case studies, and arguments that have survived longer than their authors. In the afternoons, the gardens offer a quieter surface: flowering walls under the pale paths, clipped shadows from the sheltering stone, and the hard-light bridges beyond the hedges. Your sketchbook gathers the bends of stems, lamp brackets, and the storm’s changing edge beneath the plateau.

On the second evening, the dining hall is warm with the smell of cumin and baked roots. Rashid arrives with a blue Academy envelope tucked under one arm. Aldric’s name now appears beneath Ashara’s on the copy of the request at his place.

“Administration will hear us Friday; the court stays closed until the instructor’s report arrives, but they will consider a supervised trial.”

“That is a reasonable answer,” Aldric says.

“Then bring a plan worth accepting,” Ashara says.

Rashid folds the Academy letter back along its creases and sets it beside his bowl. The request has become an appointment, not a victory, and dinner continues around it.

exchanges.player: "Good luck on Friday," I tell Rashid. I leave the preparations to him and keep to classes, reading, and sketching for the rest of the week. On Friday evening I come down to dinner and take my usual place.
exchanges.story:
Rashid acknowledges the wish with a brief incline of his head. The rest of the week settles into its own sequence of lecture rooms, reading tables, and garden benches. Your sketches acquire more of the place than its paths: the leaf-shadow beneath the elven timber by the north wall, water beading on a black stone planter after the gardeners pass, the small figures crossing the bridge in the distance.

Friday’s hearing happens without you. By dinner, Rashid has a stamped Academy notice laid beside his plate and the tired, precise look of someone who has spent an afternoon answering questions.

“The report found a cracked anchor in a hanging target, and the covered court will remain shut while they repair it. We have two supervised sessions in the east court next week, then a review.”

Ashara reads the notice over his shoulder. “You got the part that mattered.”

Aldric takes the paper when she passes it across the table. The temporary access is not the full return Rashid sought, but it gives the practice group a place to meet while the actual source of the injury is dealt with. The dining hall fills around the small outcome with serving dishes and evening conversation.

exchanges.player: "I'm glad you got somewhere to meet. Would it be all right if I came to watch one of the sessions? I'd like to see how people learn this."
exchanges.story:
Rashid keeps one finger on the edge of the Academy notice as he considers the request.

“I will ask the people who train there. It is their session, not mine to offer; if they agree, you can come next week.”

He folds the notice beneath his plate before the servers begin clearing the bowls.

exchanges.player: "Of course. Let me know what they say." I keep to my classes, reading, and sketching until Rashid has an answer. If the group is happy for me to watch, I go to the first session they invite me to and stay out of the way, watching until it ends.
exchanges.story:
Rashid does not answer immediately. The next few days pass through the familiar rooms of the Academy—seminar tables, library lamps, the gardens’ sheltered paths—until he finds you on the stair outside the common room with a folded attendance slate in one hand.

“Everyone I asked is happy for you to watch. The first supervised session is tomorrow after the last bell.”

The east court is a narrow practice yard behind the Military halls, open to the wind on one side and marked in fresh white chalk. A faculty supervisor checks the padded blades, staffs, and floor anchors before anyone begins. You stay beyond the line with the few other observers while Rashid joins eight students inside it.

The session starts with balance work and measured footwork instead of sparring. Dena Arl is among the group, her splinted wrist held close beneath the cuff of her Commerce jacket as she works the turns one-handed with a shorter student. Rashid moves between pairs when asked, then takes a staff himself when the supervisor calls for the first controlled exchanges.

Nothing in the practice is dramatic. Wooden weapons meet and stop on clear touches; partners reset their footing; the supervisor interrupts twice to correct distance and once to replace a worn grip. By the final quarter-hour, the careful rhythm has become a roomful of people breathing hard, laughing at misses, and asking for another attempt before the bell ends the session.

The equipment goes back onto the rack, attendance is recorded, and the students leave the east court in small knots of conversation. The first trial session is over.

exchanges.player: I give Caelindra the two pages. "Is there anything here you'd want to read more of?"
exchanges.story:
Caelindra takes the pages by their upper corners, careful of the ink, and reads them beneath the nearest lamp. The library goes on around her in small sounds: a chair settling somewhere below the iron stair, the dry brush of a turning page. When she reaches the end, she returns to the first sheet and reads the deputy's refusal once more.

She slides both pages back across the table. “I want the ferrywoman's choice. The bell has made it unavoidable, and the deputy makes it personal without trying to be interesting. I want to see what she believes she owes people she will never meet. Have you decided?”

exchanges.player: "No, not yet." I take back the pages and leave her to her seminar. At dinner that evening, I sit near Rashid and Ashara. I ask Rashid whether he still plans to come to my reading.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra only inclines her head, gathers the book she brought with her, and leaves you with the two pages and the library's lamp-oil hush. By dinner, the hush has become the low scrape of chairs and the bright clink of cutlery at Garvey House's long table.

Rashid has a compact sheaf of papers tucked beneath the edge of his plate, though he puts down his fork when you ask. Ashara, across from you, keeps eating as she listens.

“I still intend to. Saturday at sunset, on the west terrace. I put it in my book when you told us.”

exchanges.player: "It's moved. The porter told me this morning that the west terrace is closing for repairs. The reading is now Sunday after dinner in the east gardens." I finish eating, then take my notes to the common room and sit near the hearth. I'd like some company while I work.
exchanges.story:
Rashid takes out his book and draws a clean line through the earlier entry. “Sunday in the east gardens, then. I’ll be there.” Ashara's eyes lift at the new time and place before she returns to her dinner.

After the meal, the common room is warm with the hearth's steady work. You settle near it with your notes while the portraits over the mantel watch the room through their darkened varnish.

Several minutes later, Rashid comes in with the sheaf from dinner and a leather folio under his arm. He takes the nearest empty study table, squares the papers against its edge, and looks over. “Will I be in your way?”

exchanges.player: "Not at all. I need to concentrate, but I'm glad of the company." I work quietly for half an hour, then put the notes away and go to bed until morning.
exchanges.story:
Rashid nods once and opens his folio. For half an hour, the common room holds the fire's soft settling, the dry movement of your notes, and his pen moving in narrow deliberate lines. Once, he scratches out an entire paragraph and rearranges it on a fresh sheet; later, he pauses to count something on his fingers before writing again.

By the time you put your notes away, the sheaf has become two tidy piles and Rashid is still bent over the second. He raises two fingers in a quiet farewell without looking up.

Upstairs, your room is cool after the hearth. You sleep, and Saturday morning opens pale beyond the window, the gardens below already holding their impossible bloom.

established_events: Rowan has been at the Academy for one week. Yesterday (Thursday) at noon in the common room he told Rashid and Ashara: "I booked the west terrace for Saturday at sunset to read my new story." They both heard the place and time. No other character heard that conversation.

This morning (Friday), Rowan privately spoke to an Academy porter. The west terrace will be closed for stone repairs this weekend. They moved Rowan's reservation to the east gardens on Sunday after dinner. Rowan accepted. No one else heard them, no notice has been posted, and Rowan has told nobody else about the change.
It is now Friday afternoon. Rowan and Caelindra are alone at a library table. She agreed to read the two pages he brought before leaving for her seminar. She knows nothing about either reservation.

The two pages establish: a ferrywoman discovers that the harbor warning bell has been stolen. A deputy refuses to post a warning because the ferry company will lose passengers. The ferrywoman has not yet decided whether to search for the bell or take a boat upstream to warn the next crew. That is all Rowan has written or supplied. The thief, any accident, the deputy's later conduct and the ending are unwritten.
Rowan privately thinks that the deputy reminds him of Aldric. He has not said that to anybody or written it on the pages. Nobody can see his thoughts.

exchanges.player: I finish dinner and go to the common room. I'd like to listen to Seraphel play.
exchanges.story:
By the time the last plates have been taken away, the candles have burned down into bright little wells of wax. Rashid is still making a point to Aldric across the table with the patient precision of someone who intends to make it several more times; Ashara has one hand around her cup and is watching him with an expression that gives nothing away. Seraphel rises before the discussion reaches a conclusion.

You leave the dining hall for the common room. The fireplace has been laid but not lit, and the west window stands open above the dark gardens. Air comes through it cool and damp, carrying the smell of wet stone. A few chairs have been turned toward the window instead of the portraits.

Seraphel sits in the nearest one with a narrow river-harp across her lap, its dark wood worn pale where fingers have found the same places for years. Ysolde has taken the window seat, angled toward the garden as though she is listening for something beyond the house. Thessaly occupies one end of the sofa with both feet tucked beneath her, black eyes fixed on the harp. Ashara and Rashid arrive separately a moment later; neither brings the dining-hall argument with them.

Seraphel adjusts one of the strings.

"This begins upstream,
and does not improve
with explanation."

Her first notes are spare enough that the room seems to make space for them. They pass through the open window without forcing their way past it, a clear line of sound over the soft hiss of the garden paths after rain. Then her voice joins them, low and unadorned.

"Keep to the lower water,
where reeds remember rain.
The hill may call you upward;
the hill may call in vain.

If you have a name for home,
speak it softly to the oar.
The river has a hundred mouths
and still knows every shore."

The old song moves at an even pace, its verses turning from a ferryman's work to the villages that light lamps along the banks, then back again to the current. Seraphel's fingers make the harp sound fuller each time the refrain returns. Thessaly begins marking the rhythm against her knee after the second verse, so lightly it barely disturbs the sofa cushion. Ashara's tail rests still against the leg of her chair. Rashid leans back, his earlier sheet of paper folded in one hand and forgotten there.

At the final refrain, Seraphel lets the last chord ring beneath the window's stone arch.

"River, carry the lanterns.
River, carry the rain.
Leave us the road behind us;
bring us ourselves again."

The chord thins into the garden air. For a moment, no one speaks.

Ysolde looks from the dark paths to the harp. "The low part sounds like the water under a bridge."

"It is meant to," Seraphel says. "I am glad
it remembered how."

Rashid gives the folded paper a small, absent tap against his knee. "The chairs have missed a great deal."

Seraphel's smile returns as she looks toward you.

"There is another,
about a ferryman
who attempts to bargain with fog."

Her hand remains poised over the strings.

history.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
history.story:
The primer lies beneath the brass lamp, a red thread laid across Article Nineteen. Its few lines on heirs and bloodlines have been printed in the calm type of rules that expect to outlive whoever reads them. The desk has an old ink blot at one corner; fresh blue-black ink marks two of your fingers. At the window, the storm far below gives the gardens a brief white skeleton, then leaves them dark again.

Clothes the lawyers sent ahead occupy one end of the made bed with improbable confidence: a dark formal jacket, shirts folded sharply, boots polished enough to show the room's lamp. The patch at your charcoal coat's elbow is plainly visible beside that display. The Garvey signet catches a strip of light at your hand.

Somebody moves chairs downstairs. A woman says, "If that portrait is meant to look welcoming, it has failed."

"It is a portrait," answers a man's voice. "Its duties are limited."

"Then it has fulfilled them magnificently."

A soft knock touches the door.

"Five minutes, Garvey heir," calls another woman from the hall.
"The soup is losing heart."

"The soup is fine," the man downstairs says. A small laugh travels up the stairwell. "It has spent all day being soup."

"Then it deserves to be served
at its best," the woman at your door replies.

Her footsteps head away. Below, plates begin to clink against the long table, and the house's ground floor fills with voices you have not yet met.

history.player: I go downstairs and introduce myself. "Good evening. I'm Rowan." I take an empty seat and help myself to dinner.
history.story:
You come down into a dining hall prepared for seventeen people and occupied by eight. Candlelight lies along the varnished table. At the setting you take, steam rises from a silver tureen; you fill your bowl with clear broth and small, peppery dumplings.

"Good evening. I'm Rowan."

The woman from the hall rests a hand on the back of her chair. Warm gold light gathers at the edges of her pale hair.

"Welcome, Rowan Garvey.
Please save the soup
from a second introduction."

The tall woman with swept black-red horns gives a short nod. "Ashara vel Kothren."

"Rashid vel Amara," says the man beside her, immaculate even at dinner. "Ignore her. The soup has a long career ahead."

"Not under your supervision," Ashara says.

Across the table, the silver-haired woman sits precisely where she had been objecting to the portrait. "Caelindra Vaeyn. I have already lodged my complaint about the room."

"Ysolde Thornmantle," says the white-haired woman beside her. After a glance toward the paintings, she adds, "The portrait is not facing you."

"That makes it worse."

The small woman with black eyes leans toward her spoon. "Thessaly Morrow. It did make you change seats."

At the nearer end of the table, a golden-haired man raises his cup. "Aldric Verantus. Welcome to Garvey House."

Seraphel settles into her chair at last.

"Did the lawyers give you a schedule,
or merely a house
and a law book?"

history.player: "A schedule, thankfully. I think the lawyers would have drawn up instructions for using a spoon if they'd had more time." I eat some soup, then ask Seraphel, "What are you doing after dinner?"
history.story:
Rashid smiles over his bowl. "They would have called it a utensil protocol."

"And given it a seal," Ashara says.

The broth is hot with ginger and something citrus-bright. Seraphel's spoon pauses when you ask about the evening.

"After dinner, I mean
to play in the common room.
I have been practicing an old river-song,
and the chairs have heard it enough."

"The chairs were fortunate," Rashid says.

Seraphel looks at him. "They have offered
no opinion."

"A diplomatic audience, then."

At the other side of the table, Aldric sets down his cup. "Seraphel doesn't play badly."

"I did not say I did," she answers. "I said the chairs
have heard enough."

Ysolde lifts her gaze from the soup. "The west window in the common room is open. It carries sound into the garden." Her grey eyes rest on Seraphel. "It would suit a river-song."

Seraphel's expression softens into a brief smile.

"Then I will use the west window.
You may listen, Rowan,
if that is what you are asking."
